issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette:
Kofi, a 65-year-old man with a gentle demeanor, had worked at the same large hardware store for nearly two decades. Six months ago, that familiar space became the site of the most terrifying hours of his life. He was on shift when the hurricane made landfall, much faster and more violently than forecast. The power failed, plunging the vast, windowless building into near-total darkness, punctuated only by the shriek of the wind and the percussive slam of debris against the metal roof. For three hours, Kofi and a handful of others huddled in a stockroom, listening to the structure groan and buckle, certain the roof would collapse. The emergency exits were blocked by fallen shelving, and the sound of twisting metal convinced him there was no way out.

In the months that followed, Kofi came to a set of grim conclusions that now govern his life. He had come to believe that the world is an irredeemably dangerous place, and that the man he was before the storm—calm, easygoing, trusting—had been permanently broken. This core belief that he is irreparably damaged has hollowed out his sense of self. This conviction that he is permanently broken seems to act as a magnet for the memories of the storm, as if his mind is constantly seeking the moment the damage was done. When the intrusive memories of the hurricane strike, they feel less like recollections and more like fresh evidence of his own brokenness, a sign that his mind is no longer his own. Each time he feels the phantom vibration of the collapsing shelves, it serves as another verdict on his condition: permanently changed for the worse.

This conviction that the world is hostile and that he must always be on guard means Kofi can never truly rest. At night, he finds it nearly impossible to fall asleep, convinced that he needs to remain alert for some unseen danger. During the day, this feeling of pervasive threat manifests as a constant, exhausting watchfulness. The feeling of being on edge is so persistent that it seems to summon the traumatic memories; the more anxious and unsafe he feels, the more vividly the images of the darkened, groaning stockroom flash in his mind, pulling him back into the past. His sense of constant threat reinforces his darkest beliefs, creating a feedback loop where the feeling of danger confirms his appraisal that the world is unsafe, which in turn heightens his feeling of danger.

The memories themselves are the most tormenting aspect of his experience. They are not distant or faded; when they arrive, they are overwhelmingly present. He describes them as a film that plays over and over, and when he remembers the sound of the roof groaning, he feels he is right back in the stockroom, the metallic taste of fear in his mouth. These moments of reliving the event trigger an immediate and powerful sense of threat, making his heart pound as if the danger were happening right now rather than six months ago. The sheer "nowness" of the memory convinces him that the trauma is not over and that he is still in mortal peril.

His attempts to manage this overwhelming fear have shrunk his world. Because he is certain he must always be on guard, his every action is now dictated by a need for control and escape. When he enters any room, his first act is to locate all the exits. Back at the hardware store, a job he once enjoyed, he now insists on working only near the main entrance, constantly checking his surroundings and keeping the automatic doors in his line of sight. He believes these strategies keep him safe, but they only serve to amplify his sense of ambient threat, teaching his nervous system that even a familiar workplace is a potential death trap. This constant scanning provides daily confirmation for his belief that he is a changed man living in a hostile world, a belief which then fuels his need for these very strategies. His wife, Amina, notes that he distracts himself constantly with the television, unable to sit in silence, as if quiet would allow the memories to rush in.

It was after a severe panic attack during a simple thunderstorm, which left him crouched and shaking in the hallway of his own home, that Kofi finally agreed to seek help. He is exhausted by the constant vigilance and terrified by the feeling that he is losing himself. He fears he has been permanently ruined by what happened, but he holds onto a fragile hope that he might one day feel safe in the world again.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not describe how the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world influence or trigger his traumatic memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
